title: Cop should have 'waited for backup,' inquest told: [FINAL C Edition]
article: The Port Moody detective who shot and killed an 18-year-old coming at him with a machete should have waited for backup before resorting to deadly force on his own, a lawyer for the dead man's family said yesterday.

Less than a minute before the detective killed Keyvan Tabesh early on July 14, 2003, another Port Moody officer broadcast the warning, "Be careful, they're armed," over the police radio, an inquest into Tabesh's death heard yesterday.

Tabesh, who had two passengers in his Honda Prelude, was being chased by Port Moody police at about 1:45 a.m. He was suspected of smashing out a window of a car driven by a woman half an hour earlier in an episode of road rage.

Don Morrison, lawyer for Tabesh's family, criticized the detective, whose identity can't be published by court order, for getting involved when he should have known that backup was a short distance away.

The detective, who has been threatened since the shooting, was not in uniform and was not carrying a Taser or pepper spray. He was driving an unmarked, gold-coloured Mazda Protege equipped with a police radio.
Rather than show his police badge to let know Tabesh know who he was, the detective held up a hand-held radio as Tabesh approached his car with the machete.
"In a high-risk police chase, you need backup cover," Morrison, a former prosecutor and police complaint commissioner, said outside the inquest.
"You don't have one person going in \[to a dangerous situation\] holding up a radio."

Earlier, Sgt. Dave Wynes, the Port Moody officer who led the investigation into the killing, testified he did his best and showed his report to Vancouver police Sgt. Bob Cooper to see if there were "any stones left unturned."
His six-month murder investigation recommended no charges be laid against the detective, who has been on administrative leave with full pay for two years.
"There should be a unit set up separate from the police to investigate police shootings," Morrison told reporters.
"You need that because \[otherwise\] you may have officers investigating their colleagues," he said.
Tabesh's mother, Forough Jabalameli, said she hopes the inquest will yield answers to her questions about her son's death.
"Still, we don't know what happened," she told reporters.

Asked why her son armed himself with a machete, Jabalameli said he was fearful of being attacked following an incident seven months after the family arrived in B.C. in which he suffered a number of cuts.
